title: The most common deadlift form mistake (fishing rod syndrome)
summary: NH describes 'fishing rod syndrome', a deadlift flaw of advanced lifters where the thoracic spine rounds with protracted shoulders and disengaged lats near lockout. He blames locking the knees too early from trying to explode off the floor, and prescribes patient, constant leg pressure so knees, hips and shoulders lock together, crediting this for four injury-free years of conventional deadlifts.

claims.claim: Deadlift performance depends heavily on body shape and leverages, but anyone can find some floor pull they can do with perfect form by experimenting with stance, head position and deadlift variation.
The conventional deadlift is not for everyone; some people cannot pull it from the floor with a neutral back.
Most deadlift form critique focuses on the start (rounded back, hips shooting up), which is easy to coach and usually due to core or glute weakness or a bad setup.
Fishing rod syndrome: near lockout the shoulders protract, lats disengage and the thoracic spine rounds even if the lumbar stays straight; it plagues advanced lifters.
Thoracic rounding is less harmful than lumbar rounding but is not acceptable, and it eventually leads to lumbar rounding.
The spine follows the neck: starting with a lowered head rounds the thoracic spine, which leads to lumbar rounding.
The fishing-rod position makes lockout harder because you must uncoil a body rounded over the bar, which is why many fail deadlifts above the knee.
Strong powerlifters with this flaw often eventually injure their backs and disappear from the sport.
The cause is locking the knees too early: once knees lock, leg drive stops and the hamstrings and glutes can't help, so the upper back alone must finish the lift.
The deadlift is as much a leg press against the floor as a pull.
Fix: be patient with the knees and force production; apply constant, gradually increasing leg pressure with a neutral spine instead of exploding off the floor.
In a good deadlift the bar leaves the floor slowly but never slows down, with no hitch, and knees, hips and shoulders lock out together at the end.
In four years of conventional deadlifting NH never woke up sore-backed or had a back injury, which he credits to avoiding fishing rod form.
Unless you are a competitive powerlifter, don't trade spinal health for the few pounds a rounded-upper-back pull may give.
NH briefly pulled with a rounded upper back when obsessed with powerlifting numbers; he was slightly stronger, but his proper-form strength is catching up.

exercises.name: Conventional deadlift
cues: don't lock knees early; constant leg pressure
knees, hips and shoulders lock together
exercises.why: avoid fishing rod syndrome and back injury
